# Colab CLI

A command-line interface for Google Colab. Provision high-performance CPU, GPU, and TPU runtimes, execute local code, manage remote files, and orchestrate automated cloud pipelines — directly from your terminal.

Designed to support seamless developer productivity, headless automation, and AI agent integrations.

[Demo](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/656226a9-af13-4fdb-8eda-d7de747336a2)

> [!NOTE]
> **Platform support:** the Colab CLI currently supports **Linux and macOS** only. Windows is not supported at this time.

> [!TIP]
> Looking for in-notebook, interactive agent-assisted coding instead of a terminal workflow? See the [Colab MCP Server](https://github.com/googlecolab/colab-mcp).

---

## Key Features

* **Instant VM Provisioning:** Spin up CPU, GPU (T4, L4, G4, H100, A100), or TPU (v5e1, v6e1) runtimes in seconds.
* **Robust Code Execution:** Run local Python scripts, Jupyter Notebooks (`.ipynb`), or piped `stdin` code; launch interactive REPLs or raw TTY console shells.
* **Ephemeral Job Runner (`colab run`):** Provision a fresh VM, execute a local script with forwarded arguments, retrieve output files, and automatically tear down the runtime in a single command.
* **Activity-Based Liveness:** Sessions stay alive as long as the kernel is active, with the Colab backend automatically maintaining liveness.
* **Seamless Workspace Automation:** Mount Google Drive, authenticate Google Cloud Platform (GCP) credentials, and install dependencies with high-performance `uv` package management.
* **State & Log Archival:** Inspect local session states or export interactive history logs to standard Jupyter Notebooks, Markdown, or structured JSONL.

---

## Installation

Install the package using `uv` (recommended) or standard `pip`:

```bash
# Using uv (recommended)
uv tool install google-colab-cli

# Using pip
pip install google-colab-cli
```

---

## Quick Start

Run a CPU-based VM runtime, execute some code, and clean up:

```bash
# 1. Provision a new session
colab new

# 2. Execute code from stdin
echo "print('Hello from Google Colab!')" | colab exec

# 3. Stop and release the VM resource
colab stop
```

> [!NOTE]
> When only one session is active, you can omit the `-s, --session` option;
> the CLI automatically knows it.

## Command Index

Run `colab <command> --help` to view specific options, defaults, and detailed help.

### Session Management
| Command | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `colab new [-s NAME] [--gpu GPU] [--tpu TPU] [--high-mem]` | Allocate a new CPU, GPU, or TPU VM runtime (optionally high-RAM) |
| `colab sessions` | List all active sessions currently active on the backend |
| `colab status [-s NAME]` | Display hardware, machine shape, status, and local metadata for active sessions |
| `colab restart-kernel [-s NAME]` | Restart the active session's Jupyter kernel |
| `colab stop [-s NAME]` | Terminate a session VM and release its resources |
| `colab url [-s NAME] [--open]` | Print or open a browser URL connecting to the active session |

### Execution
| Command | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `colab run [--gpu GPU] [--tpu TPU] [--high-mem] [--keep] SCRIPT [ARGS...]` | Run a local script on a fresh VM, forwarding arguments, then release it |
| `colab exec [-s NAME] [-f FILE] [--output-image PATH]` | Execute Python code from stdin, a local `.py` file, or a `.ipynb` notebook |
| `colab repl [-s NAME] [--output-image PATH]` | Start an interactive Python REPL on the VM (exits cleanly on piped EOF) |
| `colab console [-s NAME]` | Connect to a raw interactive TTY shell (tmux) on the remote VM |
| `colab ssh [-s NAME] [--proxy-mode] [-i KEY] [--gpu GPU] [--tpu TPU] [--high-mem]` | Open an SSH shell to the runtime over WebSocket, or act as an OpenSSH `ProxyCommand` bridge for IDE remote-dev |

### File Operations
| Command | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `colab ls [-s NAME] [PATH]` | List remote files on the VM |
| `colab upload [-s NAME] LOCAL REMOTE` | Upload a local file to the VM filesystem |
| `colab download [-s NAME] REMOTE LOCAL` | Download a remote file from the VM filesystem |
| `colab rm [-s NAME] PATH` | Delete a remote file on the VM filesystem |
| `colab edit [-s NAME] PATH` | Edit a remote file in-place using your local `$EDITOR` |

### Automation & Utilities
| Command | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `colab auth [-s NAME]` | Authenticate the VM for GCP services (BigQuery, GCS, etc.) |
| `colab drivemount [-s NAME] [PATH]` | Mount Google Drive on the VM (default: `/content/drive`) |
| `colab install [-s NAME] [-r FILE \| PKG...]` | Install packages on the VM using `uv` (falls back to `pip`) |
| `colab log [-s NAME] [-n N] [-o FILE]` | View or export session history (`.ipynb`, `.md`, `.txt`, `.jsonl`) |
| `colab usage` | Show account compute-unit usage rate and balance |
| `colab pay` | Open the Colab subscription page to manage compute units |
| `colab version` | Print the installed version of the CLI |
| `colab update [--install]` | Check for a newer release (and optionally upgrade the CLI in place) |

### Global Options
* `--auth {oauth2,adc}` — Authentication strategy for the Colab API (default: `adc`).
* `-c, --client-oauth-config PATH` — Path to public OAuth client credentials configuration (default: `~/.colab-cli-oauth-config.json`).
* `--config PATH` — Path to local session metadata storage (default: `~/.config/colab-cli/sessions.json`).
* `--logtostderr` — Direct debug logging output to stderr.

## Practical Examples

### Accelerator Training with Checkpoint Retrieval

Provision an A100 GPU, install requirements, run a local training script, retrieve the resulting model weights, and terminate the VM:

```bash
colab new -s trainer --gpu A100
colab install -s trainer torch transformers
colab exec -s trainer -f train.py
colab download -s trainer checkpoints/model.bin ./model.bin
colab stop -s trainer
```

### Workspace Notebook Execution with Drive Integration

Mount Google Drive, run a local notebook against the VM kernel (outputs are written back into `report_output.ipynb`), export a Markdown log of the execution, and clean up:

```bash
colab new -s analysis
colab drivemount -s analysis
colab exec -s analysis -f report.ipynb
colab log -s analysis -o execution_log.md
colab stop -s analysis
```

## Usage Notes

* **Machine shape:** Use `--high-mem` with `colab new`, `colab run`, or `colab ssh` (when auto-creating a runtime) to request a high-RAM machine shape. Requires Colab Pro or Pro+ entitlement for supported accelerators (CPU, T4, A100, etc.). L4 and TPU runtimes ignore this flag because they only offer one shape. Machine shape is shown in `colab sessions` and `colab status`.
* **TTY Requirements:** The interactive commands `repl` and `console` require a local TTY. When running inside automated scripts or pipelines, make sure to pipe stdin (e.g., `echo "print(1)" | colab repl`) to trigger non-interactive execution modes.
* **Transparent Code Execution:** When calling `colab exec -f file.py`, the CLI reads the file locally and transmits its content to the remote kernel. You do not need to manually upload files before execution.
* **Storage & State Paths:** Session tokens and metadata are stored at `~/.config/colab-cli/sessions.json`. Global CLI settings are located at `~/.config/colab-cli/settings.json`. These can be customized or isolated via the global `--config` flag.

### Ephemeral Accelerator Jobs

Use `colab run` to run a local script on dedicated hardware without manual session lifecycle management. The CLI handles provisioning, script execution, and immediate VM teardown automatically:

```bash
# Run train.py on a T4 GPU and release the VM on completion
colab run --gpu T4 train.py
```

### Shebang Execution Support

To execute a local file directly on a remote accelerator, place the `colab run` interpreter in the shebang line:

```python
#!/usr/bin/env -S colab run --gpu L4 --keep
import torch

print("L4 GPU Available:", torch.cuda.is_available())
print("Device Name:", torch.cuda.get_device_name(0))
```

Make the script executable (`chmod +x script.py`) and run it: `./script.py`. The `--keep` option tells the CLI to preserve the session VM on completion so you can re-execute or inspect logs.

# CUDA preflight and Colab/cloud guide v1

This guide prepares future GPU work. **No CUDA sorter or GPU timing exists yet.**
The local validation machine has an NVIDIA PCI device, but no discoverable nvcc,
nvidia-smi or working CUDA driver evidence. CUDA target compilation, kernel
execution and the Colab workflow have **not been validated on a GPU**. Mocked
readiness results are tests, never hardware evidence. The existing CPU studies
remain frozen. Follow [the readiness contract](CUDA_PREFLIGHT_PROTOCOL_v1.md).

## 1. Allocate and verify an environment

In Google Colab select Runtime → Change runtime type → an available GPU hardware
accelerator, then connect. A selection is not evidence a GPU was allocated;
[Colab does not guarantee particular resources](https://research.google.com/colaboratory/faq.html).
Equivalent cloud environments need an NVIDIA GPU instance and provider-supported
CUDA image. Do not upgrade or replace hosted drivers from this guide.

Run discovery in a notebook `%%bash` cell (or ordinary cloud shell):

```sh
uname -a
python3 --version
cmake --version
command -v nvidia-smi || true
command -v nvcc || true
nvidia-smi --query-gpu=index,name,driver_version --format=csv,noheader,nounits
nvcc --version
```

Each command's status matters. Missing nvidia-smi/nvcc is expected on a CPU-only
runtime. `nvcc --version` is not a kernel test. nvidia-smi's displayed CUDA version
is the driver's supported CUDA level, not proof the toolkit is installed; see
[NVIDIA's compatibility explanation](https://docs.nvidia.com/datacenter/tesla/drivers/cuda-toolkit-driver-and-architecture-matrix.html).
Do not assume a GPU model, compute capability, toolkit version or free memory.

## 3. Prepare CPU dependencies and fallback

Create empty output parents in a source-only checkout/archive:

```sh
mkdir -p results/raw results/processed results/figures
```

Preflight itself uses Python's standard library. Full CPU tests also require CMake,
a compatible C++17 host compiler, Python3 and Matplotlib/NumPy. The local validated
stack is Python3.12.3, Matplotlib3.11.0, NumPy1.26.4, CMake3.28.3, GCC13.3.0.
Cloud images vary; confirm compatibility before installing into a dedicated venv.
These dependency-setup commands are for the cloud, **not executed locally here**:

```sh
python3 -m venv .venv
. .venv/bin/activate
python3 -m pip install 'matplotlib==3.11.0' 'numpy==1.26.4'
```

If a toolchain/venv package is missing, select a supported provider image or arrange
user-approved environment setup; preflight never installs anything. Do not use
privileged driver installation as a workaround. All following commands assume
repository cwd and the same activated venv. In separate notebook `%%bash` cells,
repeat `cd` and activation; shell variables/cwd do not persist between cells.

CPU fallback (validated project options, no CUDA compiler discovery):

```sh
cmake -S . -B build/cloud_cpu -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DMAB_ENABLE_CUDA=OFF -DMAB_ENABLE_OPENMP=OFF
cmake --build build/cloud_cpu --parallel 2
ctest --test-dir build/cloud_cpu --output-on-failure -V
```

OpenMP is optional; enable it explicitly when the image has a supported runtime.
CPU fallback never means GPU work succeeded. These commands/options were checked
locally; the cloud environment and its test outcomes remain unverified.

## 4. Save readiness evidence

Choose a previously nonexistent run directory. In a Python notebook cell:

```python
import datetime, pathlib, subprocess
stamp = datetime.datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc).strftime('%Y%m%dT%H%M%S%fZ')
run = pathlib.Path('results/raw') / ('cloud_cuda_preflight_' + stamp)
r = subprocess.run(['.venv/bin/python', 'scripts/cuda_preflight.py',
                    '--output', str(run), '--timeout-seconds', '180'], text=True)
print('preflight exit:', r.returncode, 'evidence:', run)
assert r.returncode in (0, 2), 'reporting failed; inspect diagnostics'
```

Exit0 requires actual checked device0 execution; exit2 means unavailable/unverified
CUDA and a valid completed discovery report. Read report.json and SUMMARY.txt before
continuing. COMPLETE.json means **discovery complete**, not GPU operational.
Exit1 is a reporting error; exit130 is interruption. Every attempted command has
its argv/status/stdout/stderr; skipped configure/build/runtime has a reason.
The script does not print the entire environment or PATH and redacts known secret
values/URL credentials. Review diagnostics before sharing; local paths remain.
No CUDA-enabled configuration is attempted without a working candidate nvcc and
CMake>=3.18. It uses a temporary project build and deletes that scratch directory.

## 5. Optional persistent CUDA build and smoke

**GPU/toolkit-dependent commands below have not run locally.** Proceed only after
an operational preflight. Use a separate build; MAB_ENABLE_CUDA is OFF by default.
CUDA ON requires CMake>=3.18, NVIDIA toolkit>=11.0/C++17, and a compatible host
compiler. [CMake CheckLanguage](https://cmake.org/cmake/help/v3.28/module/CheckLanguage.html)
and [FindCUDAToolkit](https://cmake.org/cmake/help/v3.28/module/FindCUDAToolkit.html)
validate compiler/toolkit independently from device execution.

```sh
cmake -S . -B build/cloud_cuda -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DMAB_ENABLE_CUDA=ON -DMAB_ENABLE_OPENMP=OFF -DMAB_ENABLE_SANITIZERS=OFF
cmake --build build/cloud_cuda --target cuda_runtime_probe --parallel 2
build/cloud_cuda/cuda_runtime_probe
ctest --test-dir build/cloud_cuda --output-on-failure -V -R '^cuda_runtime_smoke$'
```

The probe enumerates devices, records runtime/driver API versions, and tests only
device0 using a tiny kernel plus synchronized copy-back/reference check. Version
integers follow the [CUDA runtime API](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-runtime-api/group__CUDART____VERSION.html).
Probe exit77/CTest skip means unavailable enumeration or no devices; it is never a
GPU pass. Post-enumeration allocation/launch/synchronization/copy/verification failure
exits1 and fails CTest. Exit0 checks one kernel, not sorting or CUDA acceleration.
If architecture selection is needed, set CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES using the actual
GPU compute capability and toolkit-supported targets; no architecture is guessed.
Use separate CPU ASan/UBSan and CUDA builds; combining options is explicitly rejected.

Capture CPU build metadata separately (validated existing CLI):

```sh
python3 scripts/capture_environment.py --build-dir build/cloud_cpu --output results/raw/NEW_CLOUD_CPU_ENVIRONMENT.json
```

This older CPU tool deliberately says GPU not probed; use cuda_preflight/report.json
for GPU capabilities. Retain both records and identify which build produced each.
Do not mix future GPU timing rows into the current CPU schemas/plots.

## 6. Persist before runtime shutdown

Colab/cloud workspace files are ephemeral. Save the source archive/hash, preflight
report/summary/marker, exact build commands and stdout/stderr, CPU environment,
compile_commands.json and relevant build logs outside the VM. No experiment is
complete if its evidence is lost. Use fresh destinations; never overwrite studies.

Colab example (**requires Colab authorization; not locally executed**):

```python
from google.colab import drive
from pathlib import Path
import shutil
# Mount your own persistent storage; review the notebook before authorizing it.
drive.mount('/content/drive')
destination = Path('/content/drive/MyDrive/mab_evidence') / run.name
assert not destination.exists()
destination.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
shutil.copytree(run, destination)
assert (run / 'report.json').read_bytes() == (destination / 'report.json').read_bytes()
```

Also export build/environment/source evidence to exclusive sibling paths. An
alternative is downloading an evidence archive or an authenticated cloud-storage
upload configured by the user. Never embed credentials in commands/notebooks.

## Troubleshooting and next GPU milestone

- No device detected: confirm allocation/runtime type, account quota and provider
  visibility. A CPU fallback remains valid; do not report GPU results.
- GPU PCI evidence but driver unverified: missing tools/module/library is evidence
  of unavailable readiness, not proof physical hardware is broken. Use a supported
  provider GPU image or administrator-managed environment; no driver changes here.
- Driver works, nvcc absent: runtime-only images can expose a GPU without a compiler.
  Select a development image; do not infer toolkit from nvidia-smi's CUDA banner.
- nvcc works, configure/build fails: inspect recorded host-compiler/toolkit/architecture
  diagnostics; consult the installed toolkit's compatibility documentation. A compiler
  version string is not a successful target build.
- Build works, enumeration/kernel fails: preserve diagnostics and visibility variables;
  driver/toolkit/device compatibility, allocation or image architecture can matter.
  Never suppress a failed kernel as a successful smoke test.
- Colab resource interruption: export partial evidence, use a new run identifier after
  reconnecting, and never pool partial attempts into a completed study.

## Raw data, analysis and limitations

Root metadata: run/build/environment/source-review/prerequisite manifests, exact
commands and exit statuses, workspace queries, frozen-asset copies, completion or
failure/interruption marker and raw hashes. Per-dataset directory: retained
input.bin/input.json, recipe/content identity, then measurement primary.csv
(frozen31 fields), prepared/trials.csv (unchanged22 fields) and prepared/run.json,
prepared_order.csv, attempts.jsonl, calibration, resources, process RSS and markers.
The output record identities include backend, dataset, phase, trial and global
order. Four prepared values count as one invocation, never four trials.

```sh
python3 scripts/analyze_cpu_gpu.py results/raw/EXISTING_CPU_GPU_PILOT \
  --output results/processed/NEW_SUMMARY.json
```

The independent analyzer checks hashes, frozen recipes/identities/order, actual
threads, scopes, warm-ups, schema, finite timings, diagnostic workspace caps,
duplicates/missing/failed/interrupted rows and contradictory completion. Incomplete
runs are rejected by default; `--allow-incomplete` retains counts and exits1,
without paired ratios. Malformed raw data is rejected. Synthetic unit fixtures are
explicitly labelled and rejected by the public analysis CLI as performance evidence.

Summaries retain all outliers, report within-dataset median/mean/sample SD/min/max
in ns, then equally weight distinct input medians. Identical-input seed medians
collapse by their median into one input weight. Pilot groups each have one input,
so cross-dataset SD is null. Paired ratios use production GPU host-call medians
only; prepared device/transfer/E2E values never supply denominators. Resolution-
limited/nonpositive ratios are null; calibration is never subtracted. Reports are
descriptive, not rankings or significance tests. CPU/GPU run on the same VM; CPU
SMT, cloud load, frequency, cache/allocator state and thermal controls remain
confounders. No100M, broad CPU/GPU study or universal performance claim follows
from successful pilot execution.
